terms.comment: Classically a small place sacred to a god; Morgan–Owens finds it for a chapel in Dante and Egger.

terms.gloss: a place of prayer, an oratory
evidence: Vulg. Jdt. 9.1: Judith ingressa est ōrātōrium suum
terms.comment: Any place set aside for prayer, such as a room in a house or a monastery (M-O).

evidence: M-O s.v. chapel, after Latham and Niermeyer
terms.comment: Classically a little she-goat (īte domum saturae, venit Hesperus, īte capellae, Verg. Ecl. 10.77). The medieval word for a chapel comes from cappa, the cape of St Martin kept in such a shrine, and only looks the same; sacellum says it in classical Latin.

phrases.latin: est ad hanc manum sacellum: ibi angiportum propter est
phrases.english: on this side there’s a little shrine; right by it there’s an alley

sources: Lewis & Short: sacellum · Lewis & Short: oratorius · Lewis & Short: capella
Morgan–Owens, Adumbratio: s.v. chapel. Enrico Levi and Arturo Bini, Il latino come lingua viva (1937), p. 13, s.v. cappella.
